'''Kathleen C. Taylor''' (born 1942) is a chemist who won the [[Garvan–Olin Medal]] in 1989, and is notable for developing [[catalytic converter]]s for cars.<ref name="CHF">{{cite web  |title=Kathleen C. Taylor | url=http://www.chemheritage.org/discover/online-resources/chemistry-in-history/themes/public-and-environmental-health/environmental-chemistry/taylor-k.aspx|website=Chemical Heritage Foundation  |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160712164917/http://www.chemheritage.org/discover/online-resources/chemistry-in-history/themes/public-and-environmental-health/environmental-chemistry/taylor-k.aspx|archivedate=July 12, 2016}}</ref>

== Education ==
Taylor attended [[Douglass College]] at [[Rutgers University]], earning a bachelor's in [[chemistry]] in 1964. She completed her Ph.D. in [[physical chemistry]] in 1968 at [[Northwestern University]] working with Robert Burwell, Jr.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=GRC 75th Anniversary - Reflections - Transcendental GRC Principles (Lasting Memories)|url=http://www.frontiersofscience.org/reflections.aspx?category=5&essay=73|access-date=2021-10-01|website=www.frontiersofscience.org}}</ref> on the surface chemistry of [[Catalysts and Catalysed Reactions|catalysts]].<ref name="CHF" /><ref>{{Cite thesis|title=The surface chemistry of chromium oxides catalysts|date=1968|language=English|first=Kathleen C|last=Taylor|oclc = 31673583}}</ref> Following her Ph.D., she did postdoctoral research at the [[University of Edinburgh]] with [[Charles Kemball]]<ref name=":2" /> where she worked on the use of deuterium to track reactions on catalysts.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kemball|first1=C|last2=Leach|first2=H. F|last3=Skundric|first3=B|last4=Taylor|first4=K. C|date=1972-12-01|title=Reactions of 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene with deuterium oxide or deuterium over oxide catalysts|url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0021-9517%2872%2990178-9|journal=Journal of Catalysis|language=en|volume=27|issue=3|pages=416–423|doi=10.1016/0021-9517(72)90178-9|issn=0021-9517|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Career ==
In 1970, Taylor joined [[General Motors]] where she is known for her work on [[catalytic converter]]s that helped reduce pollution from car exhaust.<ref name="CHF" /> Taylor developed catalytic converters that converted nitric oxide into nitrogen, instead of ammonia, a toxin to humans.<ref name="CHF" /> In 1987, while at General Motors, Taylor also served as president of the [[Materials Research Society]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Kathleen C. Taylor|url=https://www.amacad.org/person/kathleen-c-taylor|access-date=2021-10-01|website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Past MRS Presidents|url=https://www.mrs.org/about-mrs/the-society/past-mrs-presidents|access-date=2021-10-01|website=www.mrs.org}}</ref>

When Taylor was elected a fellow of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 1995, she was cited "for the development of automotive-exhaust catalytic systems and leadership in materials battery and fuel cell research".<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Dr. Kathleen C. Taylor|url=https://nae.edu/28054/Dr-Kathleen-C-Taylor|access-date=2021-10-01|website=NAE Website}}</ref>

In a 2014 interview, Taylor described her work as an engineer and noted that she selected the field because she liked the challenge of engineering and the employment options that would available to her.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Kathleen Taylor|url=https://www.engineergirl.org/2944/Kathleen-Taylor|access-date=2021-10-01|website=EngineerGirl}}</ref> As of 2017, she was retired from General Motors,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Centennial Speaker: Dr. Kathleen C. Taylor. "Douglass and Beyond" and STEM Research Poster Session {{!}} Douglass Residential College|url=https://douglass.rutgers.edu/event/centennial-speaker-dr-kathleen-c-taylor-douglass-and-beyond-and-stem-research-poster-session|access-date=2021-10-01|website=douglass.rutgers.edu|archive-date=2021-10-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211001023118/https://douglass.rutgers.edu/event/centennial-speaker-dr-kathleen-c-taylor-douglass-and-beyond-and-stem-research-poster-session|url-status=dead}}</ref> but continued to consult at [[Columbia University]] and the [[United States Department of Energy]] on projects that reduce impacts on the environment.<ref name="CHF" />

== Personal life ==
Taylor is a painter who works in watercolors on scenes in Florida<ref>{{Cite web|title=December Artwork by Joan Tangren Reynolds & Kathleen C. Taylor|url=https://www.sanibelcommunityhouse.net/uploads/files/December%20Art%20Show%20(3).pdf|access-date=2021-10-01|archive-date=2021-10-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211001023118/https://www.sanibelcommunityhouse.net/uploads/files/December%20Art%20Show%20%283%29.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> and Massachusetts.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Gallery|first=Fort Myers Beach Art Association and|date=2016|title=Fort Myers Beach Art Association & Gallery|url=http://www.fortmyersbeachart.com/index.php|access-date=2021-10-01|website=www.fortmyersbeachart.com}}</ref>
